description: Solving linear systems, matrix factorizations, eigenvalue and singular value problems, matrix functions, norms and conditioning, and the structural helpers for building and extracting triangular and diagonal parts. These functions are built on LAPACK and BLAS and are multithreaded for large matrices.

tools.name: mldivide
tools.description: Matrix left division, the backslash operator, which solves A*x = b. MATLAB analyses the structure of A and dispatches to the appropriate algorithm: triangular solve, Cholesky, LU or QR least squares for overdetermined systems. This is the recommended way to solve any linear system and should always be preferred to computing an inverse.
tools.usage:
x = A \ b
x = mldivide(A, b)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Coefficient matrix; may be square, rectangular, sparse, banded, triangular or symmetric.

parameters.name: b
parameters.description: Right-hand side vector or matrix with as many rows as A.

tools.notes: For a rank-deficient square system MATLAB warns and returns a solution with Inf or a basic solution; use `pinv` or `lsqminnorm` for the minimum-norm solution. When solving with the same A many times, build a `decomposition` object once.

tools.name: inv
tools.description: Computes the inverse of a square matrix. It exists mainly for theoretical work and for cases where the inverse itself is the quantity of interest, such as a covariance matrix inverse used repeatedly. For solving equations, `A\b` is faster and more accurate, and MATLAB warns when the matrix is close to singular.
tools.usage: Y = inv(X)
tools.notes: inv is roughly three times the work of a backslash solve and loses accuracy. Check `rcond(A)` or `cond(A)` before trusting an inverse. Sparse inverses are usually dense, so avoid inv on sparse matrices.

tools.name: pinv
tools.description: Computes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse via the singular value decomposition, treating singular values below a tolerance as zero. Use it for rank-deficient or non-square systems where you want the minimum-norm least-squares solution. It always returns an answer without warnings, which makes it convenient but also hides conditioning problems.
tools.usage:
B = pinv(A)
B = pinv(A, tol)

parameters.name: tol
parameters.description: Singular value threshold; defaults to max(size(A))*eps(norm(A)).

tools.notes: `lsqminnorm` gives the same minimum-norm solution more efficiently and with a controllable tolerance, because it avoids forming the full pseudoinverse.

tools.name: det
tools.description: Computes the determinant of a square matrix from its LU factorization. Use it for small matrices, for characteristic polynomial work and for geometric volume and orientation calculations. It is a poor singularity test because determinants scale like the nth power of the matrix entries.
tools.usage: d = det(A)
tools.example:
det([1 2; 3 4])
det(eye(3))
A = 0.1 * eye(20);
det(A)      % tiny, yet A is perfectly conditioned
rcond(A)
tools.notes: Use `rcond` or `cond` to judge invertibility, never `det(A)==0`. For large matrices the determinant frequently overflows or underflows; work with the log determinant via `sum(log(abs(diag(U))))` from `lu`.

tools.name: rank
tools.description: Estimates the rank of a matrix as the number of singular values above a tolerance. Use it to detect linear dependence among columns, to check whether a system is consistent, and to assess the identifiability of a model. Because it is based on a tolerance, rank of nearly dependent data can be ambiguous.
tools.usage:
k = rank(A)
k = rank(A, tol)

parameters.name: tol
parameters.description: Singular value threshold; defaults to max(size(A))*eps(norm(A)).

tools.notes: rank computes a full SVD and is therefore expensive for large matrices; a rank-revealing QR (`qr` with column pivoting) is cheaper when you only need an estimate.

tools.name: trace
tools.description: Returns the sum of the diagonal elements of a square matrix, which equals the sum of its eigenvalues. Use it in matrix identities, in computing the Frobenius norm as sqrt(trace(A'*A)), and in statistics for effective degrees of freedom. It is cheap because no factorization is required.
tools.usage: b = trace(A)
tools.example:
A = magic(4);
trace(A)
sum(diag(A))
sum(eig(A))
sqrt(trace(A'*A))
norm(A, 'fro')
tools.notes: Never form A'*A just to take its trace on large data; `sum(A(:).^2)` is equivalent and far cheaper.

tools.name: norm
tools.description: Computes vector and matrix norms. For vectors it supports any p-norm plus Inf and -Inf; for matrices it supports 1, 2, Inf and 'fro'. Use it to measure residuals and errors, to normalize vectors, and to assess the size of a matrix. The matrix 2-norm requires an SVD and is the most expensive option.
tools.usage:
n = norm(v)
n = norm(v, p)
n = norm(A)
n = norm(A, 'fro')

parameters.name: p
parameters.description: For vectors: any positive real, Inf or -Inf. For matrices: 1, 2, Inf or 'fro'.

tools.notes: `normest` estimates the 2-norm of a large sparse matrix cheaply. To normalize many vectors at once use `vecnorm` or `normalize`, not a loop over `norm`.

tools.name: vecnorm
tools.description: Computes norms along a chosen dimension, returning one norm per vector rather than a single number for the whole array. Use it to get the length of every row or column at once, for example to normalize a set of feature vectors or compute pointwise distances. It supports any p-norm including Inf.
tools.usage:
N = vecnorm(A)
N = vecnorm(A, p)
N = vecnorm(A, p, dim)

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension along which the vectors lie; defaults to the first non-singleton.

tools.example:
V = [3 0; 0 4; 1 1];
vecnorm(V, 2, 2)
unitRows = V ./ vecnorm(V, 2, 2)
vecnorm(V, 1, 1)
tools.notes: For matrices, `norm(A)` returns the matrix 2-norm while `vecnorm(A)` returns column norms; the two are quite different quantities.

tools.name: cond
tools.description: Returns the condition number of a matrix with respect to inversion, the ratio of the largest to smallest singular value for the 2-norm. It quantifies how much relative error in the data can be amplified in the solution: roughly log10(cond) digits of accuracy are lost. Use it before trusting a solve on ill-conditioned data.
tools.usage:
c = cond(A)
c = cond(A, p)
tools.notes: cond(A,2) needs a full SVD; `condest` estimates the 1-norm condition number of a large sparse matrix much more cheaply, and `rcond` gives a fast reciprocal estimate.

tools.name: rcond
tools.description: Returns a fast estimate of the reciprocal 1-norm condition number, produced as a by-product of the LU factorization. Values near 1 indicate a well-conditioned matrix and values near eps indicate near-singularity. It is the quantity MATLAB reports in its 'Matrix is close to singular' warning.
tools.usage: C = rcond(A)
tools.example:
rcond(eye(4))
rcond(hilb(8))
A = [1 2; 2 4.000001];
if rcond(A) < 1e-12
    warning('ill conditioned')
end
tools.notes: rcond is an estimate, not a bound, and it is only defined for square matrices. Use `cond` when you need the true 2-norm condition number.

tools.name: eig
tools.description: Computes eigenvalues, and optionally eigenvectors, of a square matrix or of a generalized pencil (A,B). For symmetric or Hermitian input it uses a specialized algorithm that returns real eigenvalues in ascending order with orthonormal eigenvectors. Use it for vibration modes, stability analysis, principal directions and Markov chain steady states.
tools.usage:
e = eig(A)
[V, D] = eig(A)
[V, D] = eig(A, B)
[V, D, W] = eig(A)
e = eig(A, 'vector')

parameters.name: B
parameters.description: Second matrix for the generalized problem A*V = B*V*D.

parameters.name: 'vector'/'matrix'
parameters.description: Return eigenvalues as a column vector or a diagonal matrix.

tools.notes: Eigenvalues of non-symmetric matrices can be very sensitive to perturbation; check `condeig`. For a few eigenvalues of a large sparse matrix use `eigs` instead of eig.

tools.name: eigs
tools.description: Computes a small number of eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a large sparse or structured matrix using iterative Krylov methods. Specify how many you want and which part of the spectrum, such as the largest magnitude or those nearest a shift sigma. You can also pass a function handle that applies the matrix, avoiding the need to store it.
tools.usage:
d = eigs(A)
d = eigs(A, k)
[V, D] = eigs(A, k, sigma)
[V, D] = eigs(Afun, n, k)
[V, D] = eigs(___, opts)

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Number of eigenvalues to compute; defaults to 6.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: Name-value options such as Tolerance, MaxIterations, StartVector, IsFunctionSymmetric.

tools.notes: Finding interior eigenvalues near a shift requires factorizing (A - sigma*I), which can be expensive; supply a `decomposition` object or a solve function to speed it up. Convergence is not guaranteed, so check the output flag.

tools.name: svd
tools.description: Computes the singular value decomposition A = U*S*V', the most numerically reliable factorization for rank, conditioning, least squares and low-rank approximation. Called with one output it returns the singular values as a vector. The 'econ' option skips the parts of U and V that multiply zero singular values, saving a lot of memory for tall matrices.
tools.usage:
s = svd(A)
[U, S, V] = svd(A)
[U, S, V] = svd(A, 'econ')
[U, S, V] = svd(A, 0)
tools.notes: Singular values are returned in descending order. Truncating S gives the best low-rank approximation in both the 2-norm and Frobenius norm, which is the basis of PCA and image compression.

tools.name: svds
tools.description: Computes a few singular values and vectors of a large sparse or implicitly defined matrix, without forming the full decomposition. Use it for truncated SVD, latent semantic analysis, and low-rank approximations of data too large for `svd`. You can request the largest, smallest, or those nearest a value.
tools.usage:
s = svds(A)
s = svds(A, k)
[U, S, V] = svds(A, k, sigma)
[U, S, V] = svds(___, opts)

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Number of singular triplets; defaults to 6.

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: Options such as Tolerance, MaxIterations, Display.

tools.notes: Computing the smallest singular values of a sparse matrix is much harder than the largest; 'smallestnz' skips the structurally zero ones. For dense matrices that fit in memory, `svd(A,'econ')` is usually faster than svds.

tools.name: lu
tools.description: Computes the LU factorization with partial pivoting, so that P*A = L*U or A = L*U with L a permuted lower triangular factor. Use it to solve several systems with the same coefficient matrix and to compute determinants stably. For sparse matrices it also returns column permutations and a scaling vector.
tools.usage:
[L, U] = lu(A)
[L, U, P] = lu(A)
[L, U, P, Q] = lu(S)
[L, U, P, Q, R] = lu(S)
[___] = lu(S, thresh)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Square or rectangular matrix, dense or sparse.

parameters.name: thresh
parameters.description: Pivot threshold in [0,1] for sparse input; lower values favour sparsity over stability.

tools.notes: With only two outputs, L is a row-permuted triangular matrix, not truly lower triangular. For repeated solves prefer `decomposition(A,'lu')`, which handles the permutations for you.

tools.name: qr
tools.description: Computes the QR factorization A = Q*R with Q orthogonal and R upper triangular, optionally with column pivoting for rank-revealing behaviour. It underlies least-squares solving and orthogonalization, and is more stable than forming the normal equations. The economy form returns only the first n columns of Q for a tall matrix.
tools.usage:
[Q, R] = qr(A)
[Q, R] = qr(A, 0)
[Q, R] = qr(A, 'econ')
[Q, R, P] = qr(A)
R = qr(A)

parameters.name: A
parameters.description: Matrix to factor, dense or sparse.

tools.notes: With column pivoting, the magnitudes of diag(R) reveal numerical rank cheaply. `qrupdate`, `qrinsert` and `qrdelete` modify an existing factorization when the data changes slightly.

tools.name: chol
tools.description: Computes the Cholesky factorization of a symmetric positive definite matrix, returning an upper triangular R with A = R'*R. It is about twice as fast as LU and is the standard route for covariance matrices, least squares normal equations and Gaussian sampling. Requesting the second output turns failure into a flag rather than an error, which makes it a practical positive-definiteness test.
tools.usage:
R = chol(A)
L = chol(A, 'lower')
[R, flag] = chol(A)
[R, flag, P] = chol(S)

parameters.name: 'lower'/'upper'
parameters.description: Which triangle to return; 'upper' is the default.

tools.notes: chol reads only one triangle of A and does not verify symmetry, so pass a matrix you know is symmetric or symmetrize it with (A+A')/2 first. Use the flag output instead of try/catch to test positive definiteness.

tools.name: schur
tools.description: Computes the Schur decomposition A = U*T*U', where U is unitary and T is upper triangular (complex form) or quasi-triangular with 2-by-2 blocks for complex conjugate pairs (real form). It is the numerically stable foundation for matrix functions and for eigenvalue computation on non-symmetric matrices. Use `rsf2csf` to convert the real form to the complex form.
tools.usage:
T = schur(A)
[U, T] = schur(A)
[U, T] = schur(A, flag)
tools.notes: Unlike `eig`, the Schur form always exists and is computed with an orthogonal transformation, so it does not suffer when eigenvectors are nearly parallel. `ordschur` reorders the diagonal blocks.

tools.name: hess
tools.description: Reduces a matrix to upper Hessenberg form H = P'*A*P, which is zero below the first subdiagonal. This is the first step of the QR eigenvalue algorithm and makes repeated shifted solves much cheaper, which is useful for transfer function evaluation and frequency response computation. For symmetric input the result is tridiagonal.
tools.usage:
H = hess(A)
[P, H] = hess(A)
[AA, BB, Q, Z] = hess(A, B)

parameters.name: B
parameters.description: Second matrix for the generalized Hessenberg-triangular reduction.

tools.notes: Once in Hessenberg form, solving (A - s*I)x = b for many values of s costs O(n^2) instead of O(n^3) per shift, which is how frequency responses are evaluated efficiently.

tools.name: null
tools.description: Returns an orthonormal basis for the null space of a matrix, computed from the singular value decomposition. Use it to describe all solutions of a homogeneous system A*x = 0, to find redundant constraints and to parametrize the free directions of an underdetermined problem. The number of columns equals the nullity.
tools.usage:
Z = null(A)
Z = null(A, tol)
Z = null(A, 'rational')

parameters.name: tol
parameters.description: Singular value tolerance for deciding rank.

parameters.name: 'rational'
parameters.description: Return a rational basis from reduced row echelon form instead of an orthonormal one.

tools.example:
A = [1 2 3; 2 4 6];
Z = null(A)
norm(A * Z)
size(Z, 2)
rank(A) + size(Z, 2)
tools.notes: The rational form is exact for integer matrices but not orthonormal and not numerically robust. The rank-nullity theorem guarantees rank(A) + size(null(A),2) equals the number of columns.

tools.name: orth
tools.description: Returns an orthonormal basis for the range (column space) of a matrix, taken from the leading left singular vectors. Use it to remove linear dependence from a set of vectors, to build a projector onto a subspace, and to check whether two matrices span the same space. The number of columns equals the numerical rank.
tools.usage:
Q = orth(A)
Q = orth(A, tol)

parameters.name: tol
parameters.description: Singular value tolerance for deciding rank.

tools.notes: `orth` needs an SVD; for a cheap orthonormal basis of full-rank columns, `[Q,~] = qr(A,0)` is faster. `subspace` measures the angle between two subspaces.

tools.name: kron
tools.description: Computes the Kronecker tensor product, replacing each element of A with that element times the whole of B. It is the standard way to build the matrices for separable 2-D finite-difference operators, tensor-product bases and vectorized matrix equations. The result is size(A).*size(B), so it grows very quickly.
tools.usage: K = kron(A, B)

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: Matrices; the result has size m*p by n*q.

tools.notes: Always use sparse inputs for large Kronecker products: kron of two 1000-by-1000 dense matrices would need 8 TB. The identity vec(A*X*B) = kron(B',A)*vec(X) turns matrix equations into linear systems.

tools.name: cross
tools.description: Computes the vector cross product of two 3-element vectors, or of arrays of 3-vectors along a chosen dimension. Use it for normals to a plane, torque and angular momentum, and orientation calculations in 3-D geometry. Inputs must have length 3 along the operating dimension.
tools.usage:
C = cross(A, B)
C = cross(A, B, dim)

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension along which the vectors lie.

tools.notes: The cross product is anticommutative: cross(a,b) equals -cross(b,a). For angles between vectors, atan2(norm(cross(a,b)), dot(a,b)) is more accurate than acos of the normalized dot product.

tools.name: dot
tools.description: Computes the scalar dot product of two vectors, conjugating the first argument for complex input, or column-wise dot products for matrices. Use it for projections, work and energy calculations, and cosine similarity. For real vectors it is equivalent to sum(A.*B).
tools.usage:
C = dot(A, B)
C = dot(A, B, dim)

parameters.name: dim
parameters.description: Dimension along which to take the products.

tools.notes: For large matrix-matrix products use `*` rather than `dot`, which is intended for vectors. dot conjugates its first argument, so dot(z,z) equals sum(abs(z).^2).

tools.name: linsolve
tools.description: Solves a linear system while letting you declare the structure of the matrix, so MATLAB can skip the analysis that backslash performs. Use it in performance-critical code where you already know the matrix is, for example, lower triangular or symmetric positive definite. With two outputs it also returns a reciprocal condition estimate instead of warning.
tools.usage:
X = linsolve(A, B)
X = linsolve(A, B, opts)
[X, r] = linsolve(___)

parameters.name: opts
parameters.description: Struct with logical fields LT, UT, UHESS, SYM, POSDEF, RECT, TRANSA describing the matrix structure.

tools.notes: If the declared structure is wrong the answer is silently incorrect, so only assert properties you are certain of. linsolve accepts dense matrices only; for sparse systems use backslash or `decomposition`.

tools.name: lsqminnorm
tools.description: Computes the minimum-norm least-squares solution of A*x = b, choosing among the infinitely many least-squares solutions the one with the smallest norm. Use it for rank-deficient or underdetermined systems where backslash returns a basic solution with zeros. It is more efficient than forming `pinv(A)*b` and accepts a rank tolerance.
tools.usage:
X = lsqminnorm(A, B)
X = lsqminnorm(A, B, tol)
X = lsqminnorm(___, rankWarn)

parameters.name: tol
parameters.description: Tolerance for deciding the numerical rank.

parameters.name: rankWarn
parameters.description: 'nowarn' (default) or 'warn' to warn about low rank.

tools.notes: Uses a complete orthogonal decomposition rather than an SVD, so it is faster than pinv for a single right-hand side. Raising tol produces a more regularized, smaller-norm solution.

tools.name: decomposition
tools.description: Creates a reusable matrix decomposition object that can be used with the backslash operator, so the expensive factorization happens once and many right-hand sides are solved cheaply. MATLAB picks an appropriate factorization automatically or you can name one. Use it in loops and iterative algorithms where the same matrix is solved against repeatedly.
tools.usage:
dA = decomposition(A)
dA = decomposition(A, type)
x = dA \ b

parameters.name: 'CheckCondition'
parameters.description: Whether to warn about ill conditioning.

tools.notes: The object holds the factors in memory, which can be large for sparse matrices with heavy fill-in. `isIllConditioned` and `rcond` work on the object directly.

tools.name: expm
tools.description: Computes the matrix exponential using a scaling and squaring algorithm with Pade approximation, which is not the same as taking exp of each element. It gives the state transition matrix of a linear time-invariant system x' = A*x, so expm(A*t)*x0 is the exact solution at time t. Use it for discretizing continuous state-space models and for Markov generator matrices.
tools.usage: Y = expm(A)
tools.notes: expm(A) is not exp(A). For a single action on a vector, `expmv`-style Krylov methods (not in core MATLAB) or ODE integration are cheaper for large sparse A.

tools.name: logm
tools.description: Computes the principal matrix logarithm, the inverse of `expm`, using an inverse scaling and squaring method on the Schur form. Use it to recover a continuous-time generator from a discrete-time transition matrix, for example converting a sampled state-space model back to continuous time. It warns when the matrix is singular or has negative real eigenvalues, where the principal logarithm may not exist or may be complex.
tools.usage:
L = logm(A)
[L, exitflag] = logm(A)
tools.notes: A real matrix with negative real eigenvalues has no real logarithm, so expect complex output. The exitflag output reports how well the algorithm converged.

tools.name: sqrtm
tools.description: Computes the principal matrix square root X such that X*X = A, using the Schur method. Use it to whiten data with a covariance matrix, to form symmetric factorizations, and in matrix geometric means. It is different from `sqrt`, which takes the elementwise root.
tools.usage:
X = sqrtm(A)
[X, resnorm] = sqrtm(A)
[X, alpha, condest] = sqrtm(A)
tools.notes: For a symmetric positive definite matrix, `chol` gives a cheaper (non-symmetric) factor that is often just as useful. Matrices with negative eigenvalues produce a complex square root.

tools.name: diag
tools.description: Extracts a diagonal from a matrix, or builds a diagonal matrix from a vector, depending on the shape of its input. Use it to pull out eigenvalues from the D matrix returned by `eig`, to create scaling matrices, and to work with off-diagonal bands. The optional k argument selects a super- or subdiagonal.
tools.usage:
D = diag(v)
x = diag(A)
D = diag(v, k)
x = diag(A, k)

parameters.name: v
parameters.description: Vector to place on a diagonal.

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Diagonal index: 0 main, positive above, negative below.

tools.notes: Applying diag twice, `diag(diag(A))`, zeroes everything off the main diagonal. For large diagonal matrices use `spdiags` or `sparse` to avoid storing the zeros.

tools.name: tril
tools.description: Returns the lower triangular part of a matrix, zeroing everything above the kth diagonal. Use it to extract triangular factors, to build test matrices and to mask out the upper half of a symmetric matrix such as a correlation matrix. The companion `triu` does the same for the upper triangle.
tools.usage:
L = tril(A)
L = tril(A, k)

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Diagonal to keep down to: 0 includes the main diagonal, -1 excludes it.

tools.notes: `tril(true(n), -1)` is the idiomatic mask for the strictly lower triangle, which is how you extract the unique entries of a symmetric matrix.

tools.name: triu
tools.description: Returns the upper triangular part of a matrix, zeroing everything below the kth diagonal. Use it with `tril` to split a matrix into triangular parts for iterative methods such as Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel, and to clean up factorization output. It preserves sparsity for sparse input.
tools.usage:
U = triu(A)
U = triu(A, k)

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Diagonal to keep up from: 0 includes the main diagonal, 1 excludes it.

tools.notes: Because MATLAB detects triangular structure automatically, solving with a `triu` result via backslash uses a fast triangular solve.

tools.name: pagemtimes
tools.description: Performs matrix multiplication independently on each page of N-D arrays, so a stack of many small matrices is multiplied in one vectorized call. Use it for batched linear algebra such as transforming thousands of coordinate frames or applying per-sample matrices. It is much faster than looping over the third dimension.
tools.usage:
C = pagemtimes(A, B)
C = pagemtimes(A, transpA, B, transpB)

parameters.name: A, B
parameters.description: N-D arrays whose first two dimensions are the matrices.

tools.notes: Companions include `pagetranspose`, `pagectranspose`, `pageinv`, `pagemldivide` and `pagesvd` for batched operations on stacks of matrices.
